did_you_know.text: Did you know? The LORD is the one who appoints the great fish to swallow Jonah, and Jonah remains in the fish’s belly for three days and three nights.
Did you know? Even while he is inside the fish, Jonah does not stop praying; his prayer rises from a place of distress and danger.

Did you know? Jonah describes his desperate situation with the words “from the belly of Sheol”—an expression portraying his distress as though he had descended to the world of the dead, yet he still believes that the LORD hears his voice.
Did you know? In his prayer, Jonah uses powerful images of the sea—its depths, currents, breakers, and waves—to express his sense of drowning and danger.
Did you know? Although Jonah says, “I have been banished from your sight,” he does not lose hope and continues to look toward the LORD’s holy temple.
Did you know? Jonah describes the waters reaching up to his soul and seaweed wrapping around his head, vividly showing how deeply he had sunk into the sea.
Did you know? Jonah describes descending “to the roots of the mountains” and the earth closing over him, but immediately adds that the LORD brought his life up from the pit.
Did you know? According to Jonah’s prayer, when his soul was fainting within him, he remembered the LORD; this remembrance led his prayer to reach the LORD’s holy temple.
Did you know? Jonah promises to offer thanks, make sacrifices to the LORD, and fulfill his vow, concluding with the declaration: “Salvation belongs to the LORD.”

Did you know? At the end of the chapter, the LORD commands the fish, and the fish vomits Jonah onto dry land; in this way, the fish serves as an instrument of the LORD and brings about Jonah’s rescue.
